paragraphs: This paper studies why graph neural networks can generalize to unseen data, with particular attention to the structure of the graphs they process. Earlier theoretical bounds often worsen as the number of nodes grows, even though practical behavior can show the opposite. The authors address this mismatch by considering graphs sampled from an underlying manifold and analyzing their behavior in the spectral domain.

Within this setting, they prove that the generalization bounds decrease linearly with graph size on a logarithmic scale. The bounds also grow linearly with constants describing the spectral continuity of the network’s filters. This links generalization to both the sampled graph and the properties of the filters, rather than treating graph size alone as the determining factor.

The theory covers predictions about individual nodes and whole graphs. It also identifies a design tradeoff: restricting discriminability is necessary for better generalization within the analysis. Experiments using synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the proposed bounds, connecting the theoretical account to observed behavior.
icml-2025-a-manifold-perspective-on-the-.tldr: A manifold-based analysis connects GNN generalization to graph size and filter continuity, explaining behavior that earlier bounds missed.

paragraphs: CodeSync addresses a persistent problem for language models that write software: library interfaces change after the model’s training data was collected. A model can therefore produce outdated code that fails to execute or uses less safe or efficient implementations. The paper treats keeping code knowledge current as a distinct capability that needs both updated data and direct evaluation.

The authors introduce a data engine that identifies obsolete code patterns and gathers current updates from Python libraries. They use it to build CodeSyncBench, covering changes to 220 APIs across six libraries. The benchmark contains 3,300 test cases across three evaluation tasks, alongside 2,200 training examples designed for instruction tuning that accounts for updates.

Experiments with 14 language models find that adapting to changing code remains difficult, even when using updating methods such as DPO, ORPO, and SimPO. The contribution is therefore both infrastructure and evidence: CodeSync supplies material for studying updates, while the benchmark exposes a continuing gap in models’ ability to follow software evolution.
icml-2025-codesync-synchronizing-large-l.tldr: CodeSync collects changing library knowledge and provides a benchmark showing that language models still struggle to keep generated code current.

paragraphs: This paper uses visual generative models to understand images by asking which scene description would best reproduce an observed picture. The task becomes a search for the model’s conditioning parameters. Instead of using generation only to create images, the method uses the relationship between scene parameters and generated content to infer what an image contains.

The authors build the generative model compositionally, combining smaller models that describe pieces of a scene. This design is intended to support inference on images substantially different from the training examples. By representing a scene through its parts, the method can accommodate new combinations instead of depending entirely on familiar complete scenes.

The paper demonstrates inference of object sets, including generalization to scenes containing more objects and unfamiliar shapes. It also demonstrates inference of global scene factors with generalization to new scenes. Finally, the approach is applied directly to existing pretrained text-to-image models for zero-shot perception of multiple objects, showing how generative capabilities can support scene analysis without task-specific examples in that setting.
icml-2025-compositional-scene-understand.tldr: Compositional generative models infer scene properties by finding the conditions that best explain an image, with demonstrated generalization to unfamiliar scenes.

paragraphs: DyPolySeg tackles semantic segmentation of point clouds when only a small set of labeled support examples is available. These examples provide category prototypes used to identify points in an unlabeled query. The paper targets two difficulties: capturing enough geometric structure and connecting category information between the support and query sets. It also seeks to avoid the domain shifts and additional training time associated with pre-training.

The proposed network learns without a separate pre-training stage. Its dynamic polynomial convolution combines a low-order component for flatter local geometry with a dynamic higher-order component for finer geometric detail. A Mamba block adds global context, allowing the representation to incorporate information beyond individual local neighborhoods.

A lightweight prototype completion module further connects the support and query representations. It uses self-enhancement and interaction between the two sets to reduce structural differences that hinder matching. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on S3DIS and ScanNet. Together, the results support combining richer geometric modeling with prototype refinement for segmentation from limited labeled examples.
icml-2025-dypolyseg-taylor-series-inspir.tldr: DyPolySeg combines dynamic polynomial geometry features and prototype completion for leading few-shot point cloud segmentation without pre-training.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training data while preserving performance on data that should be retained. This paper considers the harder source-free setting, where the original training data cannot be accessed. Existing approaches in this setting can require expensive distillation and retraining, motivating a method that addresses both data availability and computational cost.

The proposed DSDA framework begins by synthesizing data. Its accelerated energy-guided synthesis stage uses Langevin dynamics to model the training distribution, with Runge–Kutta methods and momentum introduced to improve efficiency. This stage supplies a synthetic basis for the subsequent unlearning process without requiring access to the original examples.

The second stage uses discrimination-aware multitask optimization. It refines the feature distribution associated with retained data and reduces conflicts between gradients from different unlearning objectives. Experiments on three benchmark datasets report better performance than existing unlearning methods, supporting the framework’s effectiveness and efficiency. The central contribution is coordinating synthetic data generation with optimization that accounts for competing unlearning goals.
icml-2025-efficient-source-free-unlearni.tldr: DSDA combines accelerated data synthesis with multitask optimization to perform effective, efficient unlearning without the original training data.

paragraphs: Federated causal structure learning combines information from datasets held by separate clients to infer causal relationships. Many methods assume that every client measures the same variables. This paper studies the more complicated case in which clients observe overlapping but different sets of variables, where non-overlapping variables can introduce misleading dependencies into the learned relationships.

The authors first develop theory for detecting these spurious dependencies and assessing whether learned relationships are correct. They then distinguish correctness from quality across multiple local graphs. Relationships that satisfy both criteria are treated as stable. This shifts attention from judging an entire client graph with a single overall score to evaluating the individual relationships it contributes.

A two-level priority selection strategy aggregates local updates into a global causal graph spanning the integrated variables. The approach considers both causal relationships and the absence of such relationships when deciding what to combine. Experiments on synthetic, benchmark, and real-world data demonstrate effectiveness, supporting relationship-level aggregation when clients do not share an identical measurement space.
icml-2025-federated-causal-structure-lea.tldr: The method combines client causal graphs with different variable sets by detecting spurious dependencies and prioritizing stable individual relationships.

paragraphs: Black-box discrete prompt learning improves text prompts without accessing a language model’s parameters or gradients. This makes it suitable for cloud-hosted models, but each interaction with the service carries a query cost. Federated learning can bring together information from different clients, yet the paper argues that earlier federated prompt-tuning research overlooked this substantial expense.

The authors analyze query efficiency in federated black-box prompt learning. Their analysis finds that modifying FedAvg so that only one client participates in each round achieves optimal query efficiency in the studied setting. They call this strategy FedOne and build a discrete prompt-learning framework around it.

The key practical implication is that the number of clients active in a round should be considered alongside the value of their training contributions. FedOne organizes participation around the cost of querying the shared cloud model. Numerical experiments across several aspects of the framework show significant improvements in query efficiency, consistent with the theoretical result. The claim concerns this prompt-learning setting and its query objective.
icml-2025-fedone-query-efficient-federat.tldr: FedOne activates one client per round to achieve theoretically optimal query efficiency in the studied federated black-box prompt-learning setting.

paragraphs: Image-to-video generation begins with an image that already contains useful visual information. The paper argues that a diffusion process organized around transforming noise into data is inherently mismatched with this starting point and may produce suboptimal results. FrameBridge instead models a transition from the supplied frame to a sequence of frames using a bridge-based, data-to-data generation process.

The authors develop separate techniques for two training situations. SNR-Aligned Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained diffusion model into a bridge model, allowing FrameBridge to benefit from existing text-to-video models. When training from scratch, a proposed neural prior further improves synthesis quality. These components support using the bridge formulation with either inherited model knowledge or new training.

Experiments conducted on WebVid-2M and UCF-101 report better quality than the diffusion counterpart. The reported FVD values are 95 versus 192 in zero-shot evaluation on MSR-VTT and 122 versus 171 in non-zero-shot evaluation on UCF-101. The experiments also support the benefits of the fine-tuning technique and neural prior within bridge-based generation.
icml-2025-framebridge-improving-image-to.tldr: FrameBridge models image-to-video generation as a frame-to-frames bridge process and reports better synthesis quality than its diffusion counterpart.

paragraphs: Retrieval-augmented generation gives language models access to external knowledge, but retrieval alone may not uncover specialized information or connect it through several reasoning steps. This paper addresses that gap by decomposing complex questions in a way that responds to the knowledge already found. The aim is to build a coherent rationale while extracting relevant information from segmented source data.

The approach has four interacting components. A knowledge atomizer extracts atomic questions from raw data, and a query proposer suggests follow-up questions relevant to the original inquiry. An atomic retriever locates knowledge through alignments at this smaller scale. An atomic selector then uses the retrieved information to decide which follow-up questions should be asked.

This creates an iterative process in which acquired knowledge guides further decomposition and reasoning. Evaluations across several benchmarks, particularly those requiring multihop reasoning, report improvements of up to 12.6% over the second-best method. That maximum reported gain supports the approach’s potential for complex knowledge-intensive tasks, while preserving the distinction between its strongest result and performance across all evaluated cases.
icml-2025-from-complex-to-atomic-enhanci.tldr: Knowledge-aware decomposition uses atomic questions and retrieved evidence to guide follow-up reasoning, improving performance on complex retrieval-augmented tasks.

paragraphs: Reward models help align language models by evaluating their responses. Standard training commonly treats this as a discriminative problem and relies on labeled human preferences. GRAM explores a broader training route: use unlabeled data as well as preference labels to build a reward model that can transfer across tasks.

The method starts with large-scale unsupervised training of a generative reward model and then applies supervised fine-tuning. The paper also analyzes label smoothing, showing that its use corresponds to optimizing a regularized pairwise ranking loss. This connects the generative formulation to discriminative reward modeling through a shared class of objectives, providing a theoretical interpretation of how the model learns to compare responses.

The resulting foundation reward model is intended to serve many tasks with little or no additional fine-tuning. Experiments demonstrate generalization in response ranking, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and adaptation through fine-tuning, with significant gains over several strong baselines. These findings support combining broad unsupervised learning with targeted supervision to improve the reach of reward models.
icml-2025-gram-a-generative-foundation-r.tldr: GRAM combines unsupervised generative training and supervised preference learning to produce a reward model that generalizes across several tasks.

paragraphs: Trajectory representation learning compresses movement data into vectors that can support later analysis. Existing methods often use either a free-space perspective or a road-network perspective, limiting the spatial and temporal information they capture. They also commonly train for individual tasks. GTR addresses both issues with a shared framework designed for pre-training, adaptation, and changing trajectory data.

Its multi-view encoder captures complementary features of trajectories. During pre-training, a spatial and temporal mixture of experts dynamically combines information about where movement occurs and how it develops over time. The pre-train-and-fine-tune structure then supports adapting these representations to different analysis tasks, rather than requiring each task to begin with an entirely separate learning process.

GTR also introduces an online frozen-hot updating strategy to update the representation model efficiently as trajectory data changes. Experiments on two real-world datasets report consistent improvements over 15 state-of-the-art methods across six trajectory-analysis tasks. The results support the value of combining multiple views, dynamic feature fusion, and ongoing updating within a reusable representation framework.
icml-2025-gtr-a-general-multi-view-and-d.tldr: GTR learns reusable trajectory representations through multiple views, dynamic spatial-temporal fusion, and efficient online updating.

paragraphs: Learning hidden relationships from data becomes complicated when some structure is already known. Existing methods can struggle to incorporate known edges, constraints on node connections, or overall sparsity without destabilizing training or contradicting their probabilistic setup. Soft-Gated Structural Inference addresses this problem within a variational autoencoder framework that combines prior knowledge with data-driven learning.

The method uses learnable edge masks with soft gating so that gradients remain available during optimization. It handles deterministic edges through cloning-clamping, avoiding conflicts with stochastic inference. Adaptive regularization balances the influence of domain constraints against the information learned from data. Known edges are excluded from stochastic inference, redirecting modeling capacity toward uncertain relationships.

Across 16 datasets, the authors report edge-recovery improvements of up to 9% AUROC over baselines, stable training, and 94.2% AUROC in larger-graph evaluations. These findings support incorporating structural knowledge directly into inference rather than treating every interaction as equally uncertain. The framework is presented as a route toward more interpretable and robust discovery of relationships in dynamical systems.
icml-2025-guided-structural-inference-le.tldr: SGSI integrates known structural constraints into a variational model while preserving stable training and focusing inference on uncertain edges.

paragraphs: This paper evaluates whether visual generative models produce content resembling characters protected by intellectual property rights. The authors find striking similarities in outputs from leading image and video generators. Such outputs can arise when prompts name a character directly, but also when prompts only describe the character’s distinguishing features. The finding raises potential legal concerns about how these models respond to descriptive requests.

The proposed defense changes the generation process itself. It identifies content that may infringe protected character rights and applies guidance during diffusion to mitigate that content. Because the intervention operates during generation, it does not require retraining or fine-tuning the pretrained model.

Experiments involving well-known characters, including Spider-Man, Iron Man, and Superman, demonstrate the defense’s effectiveness. The contribution connects an evaluation problem with a generation-time mitigation strategy: resemblance can emerge from indirect descriptions, so intervention considers the generated content as well as the prompt. The reported evidence concerns identifying and reducing potentially infringing character outputs, with resemblance framed as a source of potential legal concern.
icml-2025-how-to-evaluate-and-mitigate-i.tldr: The paper documents protected-character resemblance in generated visuals and proposes diffusion-time guidance to mitigate potentially infringing outputs without retraining.

paragraphs: Weakly supervised video anomaly detection must locate anomalous events in time using labels that describe an entire video. Without annotations for individual frames, a detector may identify only part of an event. LEC-VAD focuses on recovering more complete event intervals, making the start and end of an anomaly central to the learning problem.

The method uses a dual structure to connect vision and language through both category-aware and category-agnostic semantics. This allows it to represent information tied to particular anomaly types alongside information that is not category-specific. Semantic regularities built around an anomaly-aware Gaussian mixture guide the learning of event boundaries and more complete event instances.

A second component uses a memory bank and prototype learning to enrich the short text descriptions associated with anomaly categories. More expressive descriptions strengthen the language information available to the detector. Evaluations on XD-Violence and UCF-Crime report substantial advances over current state-of-the-art methods. The findings support jointly improving temporal boundary learning and the semantic descriptions used to recognize anomalous events.
icml-2025-learning-event-completeness-fo.tldr: LEC-VAD combines vision-language semantics, boundary learning, and enriched category descriptions to locate more complete anomalous events from video-level labels.

paragraphs: Retrosynthesis plans how to make a target molecule by working backward through valid reactions to simpler precursors. Even when a model can predict useful individual reaction steps, searching for a complete route remains difficult because the number of possible pathways grows rapidly. This paper investigates whether language models’ chemical knowledge can help with that constrained, multistep planning problem.

The authors introduce an efficient way to encode reaction pathways and a search strategy that operates at the route level. This changes the unit of decision-making from individual reactant predictions to synthesis pathways. The approach uses language models to augment the planning process, aiming to navigate the large space of possible routes more effectively.

Comprehensive evaluations are reported to show strong retrosynthesis-planning performance. The method also extends to synthesizable molecular design, connecting the choice of a molecule with the question of how it could be made. The contribution is therefore a way to organize chemical knowledge and route search together, with demonstrated applicability to both planning synthesis and designing molecules around synthesis considerations.
icml-2025-llm-augmented-chemical-synthes.tldr: An LLM-augmented route-level search approach supports multistep retrosynthesis planning and extends to synthesizable molecular design.

paragraphs: MaskTwins studies how masking images can help segmentation models adapt across domains. Earlier approaches connected masked image modeling to consistency regularization but largely treated masking as another input deformation. This paper instead analyzes masked reconstruction as a sparse signal reconstruction problem, providing a theoretical basis for choosing how images should be masked.

The authors prove that a dual form of complementary masks has superior capabilities for extracting features that do not depend on the image domain. Their framework applies complementary masking during the main training process and encourages predictions from the differently masked images to agree. This consistency requirement helps uncover structural patterns that remain useful across different domains.

Experiments on natural and biological image segmentation report improvements over baseline methods. The framework achieves these results without a separate pre-training stage, integrating reconstruction and segmentation learning end to end. Its contribution combines a theoretical explanation for complementary masking with a practical training design, supporting the use of masking to learn shared structure rather than treating it only as input disruption.
icml-2025-masktwins-dual-form-complement.tldr: MaskTwins uses theoretically motivated complementary masks to learn domain-invariant segmentation features directly during training.

paragraphs: Human preferences are diverse and can conflict, making alignment with a single reward model incomplete. Approaches that train with multiple reward dimensions can address this diversity, but their reinforcement-learning process can be expensive and unstable. Mixing Preference Optimization tackles the problem by combining policies that have already been aligned to individual objectives.

MPO is a post-processing framework that creates a unified policy through a log-linear combination of existing policies. It computes their mixing weights using batch stochastic mirror descent. The core decision is how much influence to assign to each available policy, allowing the method to reuse prior alignment work instead of performing alignment from scratch.

The paper presents MPO as an alternative to multi-objective RLHF and MaxMin-RLHF. Empirical results show balanced performance across different preferences, with performance that matches or exceeds existing models while substantially reducing computational costs. These findings support policy combination as an efficient way to handle competing preferences, with the reported balance arising from the tested mixtures and learned weights.
icml-2025-mpo-an-efficient-post-processi.tldr: MPO efficiently balances diverse preferences by learning how to combine existing single-objective policies after alignment.

paragraphs: This paper investigates in-context learning for data whose outcomes are categories. It examines attention-based inference through the lens of functional gradient descent, connecting a network’s computations to a sequence of optimization steps. The goal is to give a precise account of how an attention architecture can carry out learning from context for categorical observations.

The authors construct a network from attention blocks, each containing self-attention followed by cross-attention, together with skip connections. They show that this model can exactly implement multiple steps of functional gradient descent during in-context inference. The result establishes an exact computational correspondence for the proposed architecture, giving its attention operations a specific optimization interpretation.

The theoretical analysis broadens several assumptions used in earlier work, including the range of attention mechanisms covered. Empirical demonstrations use synthetic data, image classification, and language generation. These examples show the framework in several categorical-data settings, while the central theoretical claim concerns the constructed network’s ability to perform the specified inference procedure exactly.
icml-2025-on-understanding-attention-bas.tldr: A constructed attention network exactly implements multistep functional gradient descent for in-context inference with categorical outcomes.

paragraphs: Training language models with fewer bits can reduce arithmetic costs, but four-bit floating-point precision creates substantial representation and quantization errors. This paper introduces an FP4 training framework designed to manage those errors while maintaining useful model accuracy. It extends the pursuit of lower-precision training beyond the already demonstrated feasibility of FP8.

Two components address the main training difficulties. A differentiable quantization estimator supports accurate weight updates despite quantization. An outlier clamping and compensation strategy prevents activation collapse. The framework also combines different numerical precisions and applies vector-wise quantization to improve stability, so its FP4 approach operates within a broader mixed-precision training scheme.

Experiments report accuracy comparable to BF16 and FP8 with only minimal degradation. The evaluations scale to models with 13 billion parameters trained on as many as 100 billion tokens. These findings demonstrate that the proposed numerical safeguards can make FP4 training viable at the reported scale. The paper positions this framework as groundwork for efficient training on emerging hardware that supports FP4 operations.
icml-2025-optimizing-large-language-mode.tldr: An FP4 training framework controls quantization errors and instability, achieving accuracy close to BF16 and FP8 at the reported model scales.

paragraphs: Maximal ancestral graphs represent causal relationships among observed variables when some variables are hidden. Observational data generally identifies an equivalence class of such graphs, represented by a partial ancestral graph, leaving some relationships uncertain. Listing the compatible graphs allows downstream analyses to work with these unresolved possibilities.

The paper introduces a listing method with polynomial delay: the time required to produce each successive graph is polynomial. It recursively introduces individual pieces of structural background knowledge and applies new orientation rules. These rules are sound and locally complete for the relevant knowledge, enabling the method to output every graph in the equivalence class and exclude graphs outside it.

The authors also examine the broader problem of incorporating general background knowledge. Two counterexamples show that existing rules, including their new ones, are not complete for that broader purpose, motivating two additional rules. Experiments validate the listing method’s efficiency. The computational guarantee applies to the delay between outputs, which matters when the set of compatible causal graphs itself may be large.
icml-2025-polynomial-delay-mag-listing-w.tldr: New orientation rules enable exhaustive listing of compatible maximal ancestral graphs with polynomial delay between outputs.

paragraphs: Binary quadratic distributions appear in discrete optimization and probabilistic inference, but drawing samples from them can be difficult. Stochastic localization has theoretical support in continuous settings, where Markov chain Monte Carlo methods estimate the posterior expectations it needs. Extending that reasoning to discrete samplers requires overcoming different convergence challenges.

The authors apply stochastic localization to general binary quadratic distributions. They prove that, after a certain number of iterations, the external fields of the constructed posterior distributions tend to infinity almost everywhere. The posteriors consequently satisfy Poincaré inequalities with probability close to one, leading to polynomial-time mixing. This gives a route to efficient sampling even when the original distribution may lack fast-mixing properties.

The analysis covers a broad range of discrete samplers based on Glauber dynamics and Metropolis-Hastings algorithms. Experiments use quadratic unconstrained binary objectives associated with maximum independent set, maximum cut, and maximum clique problems. Consistent efficiency improvements across samplers support the practical value of transforming the posterior sampling problem through localization.
icml-2025-sampling-from-binary-quadratic.tldr: Stochastic localization produces favorable posterior sampling conditions for general binary quadratic distributions, with theoretical guarantees and empirical efficiency gains.

paragraphs: TimeDART learns representations of time series without relying on labels during pre-training. The paper focuses on a difficulty in existing approaches: capturing both the long-term evolution of a sequence and its subtle local patterns within one framework. Representations that account for both can be more useful across subsequent analysis tasks.

The method first divides the sequence into patches and uses a causal Transformer encoder to model trends from left to right. It then introduces a diffusion process, with forward diffusion and reverse denoising, to capture finer local structure. Autoregressive optimization brings these components together, combining the sequence-level modeling of the Transformer with the local modeling supplied by denoising.

Experiments on public datasets evaluate the learned representations for forecasting and classification. TimeDART consistently outperforms the previous methods included in those comparisons. The results support unifying the two generative approaches for time-series pre-training: the framework is designed to learn evolving trends and fine detail together, and its usefulness is demonstrated across both future prediction and sequence categorization.
icml-2025-timedart-a-diffusion-autoregre.tldr: TimeDART combines autoregressive Transformers and diffusion denoising to learn time-series representations that capture global trends and local detail.

paragraphs: TruthFlow addresses hallucinations by adjusting a language model’s internal representations. Existing intervention methods often apply one shared correction vector to every query. The paper argues that this uniform adjustment limits effectiveness when questions differ substantially, motivating corrections that respond to the particular query being answered.

The method uses flow matching to train a flow model that learns query-specific correction vectors. These vectors move representations from hallucinated states toward truthful states. During inference, the trained flow model produces the corresponding corrections and applies them to improve the truthfulness of the language model’s output. The learned intervention therefore varies with the input rather than using a single correction for all requests.

Experiments on TruthfulQA report significant improvements in open-ended generation across several advanced language models. The trained correction model also performs effectively on other hallucination benchmarks that were unseen during training. These results support both the usefulness of query-specific interventions and their ability to transfer across the evaluated benchmarks, without implying that every generated answer becomes truthful.
icml-2025-truthflow-truthful-llm-generat.tldr: TruthFlow learns query-specific representation corrections that improve language-model truthfulness and transfer to unseen hallucination benchmarks.

paragraphs: Recommendation from implicit feedback lacks explicit negative examples. A missing interaction does not establish that a user would dislike an item, yet negative sampling often treats unlabeled interactions that way. This can incorrectly label potential positives as negatives and damage learning. PURL approaches the problem by treating the available evidence as weak supervision.

The framework is model-agnostic and eliminates the need to supply negative samples. However, its unbiasedness depends on accurately estimating the class prior, which describes the underlying balance of classes. This dependence is central to the approach: avoiding negative sampling still requires estimating a quantity needed to interpret the positive and unlabeled data correctly.

The authors introduce Progressive Proximal Transport to estimate that prior by minimizing a proximal transport cost between positive and unlabeled samples. Experiments on three real-world datasets show improved recommendation quality. The findings support pairing weakly supervised recommendation with explicit prior estimation, while the theoretical unbiasedness claim remains conditional on the accuracy of that estimate.
icml-2025-unbiased-recommender-learning-.tldr: PURL learns recommendations without negative samples, with unbiasedness conditional on accurate class-prior estimation using its proposed transport method.

paragraphs: WGFormer predicts molecular ground-state conformations, the arrangements of atoms that minimize energy. Such predictions matter for applications including docking and molecular property prediction. Traditional energy-based simulation can be slow, while learning-based approaches offer computational efficiency but can lose accuracy and interpretability. The paper aims to connect the strengths of these two strategies.

The method uses an auto-encoding framework. A proposed SE(3)-Transformer encodes low-quality conformations, and a multilayer perceptron decodes corresponding ground-state conformations. The Transformer’s architecture corresponds to Wasserstein gradient flows: it improves conformations by minimizing an energy function defined over latent mixture models of atoms. This gives the learned transformation an explicit connection to energy-based optimization.

Extensive experiments report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art competitors. The authors also attribute improved interpretability to the architecture’s relationship with the energy-minimization process. The contribution is a learned conformation predictor whose internal design follows a structured optimization principle, connecting efficient prediction with an account of how atomic arrangements are refined toward lower-energy states.
icml-2025-wgformer-an-se-3-transformer-d.tldr: WGFormer connects a learned molecular conformation predictor to Wasserstein gradient flows, improving reported accuracy and interpretability.
